canonical_statement: The policy applies to pediatric and adult patients at risk for or with extravasation of intravenous or intraarterial medications or infusions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Purpose: To outline the care of the pediatric or adult patient at risk for or with an extravasation of intravenous or intraarterial medications and/or infusion.

canonical_statement: The policy states that extravasation can cause significant soft-tissue injury and that prompt treatment is imperative because tissue damage begins at the time of extravasation; some cases require weeks to months of follow-up.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Extravasation of certain medications can cause significant soft tissue injury... prompt treatment is imperative... Some extravasations require extended (weeks to months) follow-up.

canonical_statement: To reduce extravasation, the policy recommends administering certain irritant and vesicant medications through a CVAD or PICC whenever possible and appropriate and checking with pharmacy about peripheral venous access suitability.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: To reduce the incidence of extravasations, certain irritant and vesicant medications should be administered in a CVAD or PICC whenever possible and appropriate. Check with pharmacy to determine if medications are appropriate for peripheral venous access.

canonical_statement: RNs and LPNs may treat extravasation infusions after demonstrating the General Medication Administration Competency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: RNs and LPNs may treat extravasation infusions after demonstrating competency. Competency/Skills: General Medication Administration Competency

canonical_statement: The policy defines infiltration as unintentional leakage of a nonvesicant solution into surrounding tissue and notes that delayed recognition can lead to significant edema and vascular compromise.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Infiltration – Unintentional leakage of a nonvesicant solution into surrounding tissue. Infiltrations can cause significant edema and vascular compromise if not recognized early.

canonical_statement: The policy defines extravasation as leakage of a vesicant solution from the vein into surrounding tissue.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Extravasation – Leakage of a vesicant solution from the vein into the surrounding tissue

canonical_statement: The policy defines a vesicant as a solution capable of injuring surrounding tissue, including blistering, tissue sloughing, or necrosis, and emphasizes early treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Vesicant – Solution that can cause injury or damage to surrounding tissue. Vesicants can cause blistering, tissue sloughing, or necrosis. Early treatment is important to minimize tissue damage.

canonical_statement: The policy describes subcutaneous hyaluronidase around the site as a treatment intended to reduce tissue damage when given within 2 hours for specified medications and states that it increases fluid absorption 3- to 5-fold.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Hyaluronidase injection - Administered subcutaneously around the injection site to reduce tissue damage when treatment occurs within 2 hours of extravasation of specific medications. When hyaluronidase is used to treat IV medication extravasations, the increased rate of absorption of fluid is 3-5 fold.

canonical_statement: The policy describes subcutaneous phentolamine around the extravasation site within 12 hours as a local vasodilator used to prevent or treat dermal ischemia, necrosis, and sloughing for selected medications.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Phentolamine injection - Administered subcutaneously around the injection site to reduce tissue damage when treatment occurs within 12 of the extravasation. Phentolamine causes local vasodilation thus, it is effective in the prevention and treatment of dermal ischemia, necrosis and sloughing that occurs when select medications extravasate.

canonical_statement: When extravasation is suspected, the policy directs clinicians to stop the infusion.
After stopping the infusion, the policy directs clinicians to attempt aspiration of fluid from the IV catheter at the hub.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: B. Attempt to aspirate fluid from the IV catheter at the hub.

canonical_statement: The policy directs clinicians to assess the size of the affected area and outline it with a marker.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 1. Size of affected area. Outline the area with a marker.

canonical_statement: The policy directs clinicians to identify the name, volume, and concentration of the extravasated drug or drugs.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: 2. Name, volume and concentration of extravasated drug(s).

canonical_statement: The policy directs clinicians to assess color, edema, pain, skin breakdown, and drainage at the extravasation site every 2 hours after the event until signs and symptoms resolve.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Color (redness or blanching), edema, pain, skin breakdown, and drainage at the extravasation site every 2 hours after the event until signs and symptoms resolved.

canonical_statement: The policy directs a neurovascular assessment of the affected limb, including pulse, capillary refill, color, temperature, sensation, and joint movement, with provider notification for any alteration.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Complete a neurovascular assessment of affected limb including pulse presence, capillary refill time, color, temperature, sensation and joint movement. Notify the provider of any alterations to neurovascular status.

canonical_statement: The policy recommends elevating the affected site if possible.
The policy directs clinicians not to apply pressure to the extravasation site.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: E. Do not apply pressure to the extravasation site.

canonical_statement: The policy directs clinicians to notify the provider to determine whether an antidote or other treatment is needed and states that pharmacist-provider consultation can help select treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Notify Provider to determine need for antidote/treatment. Consultation with a pharmacist and provider can help determine appropriate antidote or treatment.

canonical_statement: If the extravasated medication is not listed in the treatment chart, the policy directs clinicians to contact the pharmacist about the need for an antidote or treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: If the medication that was infusing is not listed in the chart below, and extravasation is suspected, contact your pharmacist about the need for an antidote/treatment

canonical_statement: The policy directs clinicians to remove the IV only when it is no longer necessary for antidote administration, with an ICN/SCN exception directing immediate catheter removal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Only remove the IV if no longer necessary for Antidote (see below) a. ICN/SCN: Remove Catheter immediately

canonical_statement: For hyaluronidase treatment, the policy specifies 150 units/mL, five 0.2 mL subcutaneous injections around the affected-area circumference using a new 25-gauge needle for each injection (0.1 mL injections in ICN/SCN), with administration most effective within 1-2 hours and a dry gauze dressing afterward.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Use hyaluronidase 150 units/ml for administration... Prepare 5 injections of 0.2 mL each. ICN/SCN: 0.1 mL... Most effective if administered within 1-2 hours... Apply dry gauze dressing to affected area.

canonical_statement: For ICN/SCN phentolamine treatment, the policy limits the dose to 0.1 mg/kg or 2.5 mg total, dilutes 5 mg in 10 mL 0.9% sodium chloride to 0.5 mg/mL, and administers small 0.1-0.2 mL subcutaneous divided doses around the site within 12 hours.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dose should not exceed 0.1mg/kg or 2.5 mg total... Dilute 5 mg in 10 ml 0.9% Sodium Chloride injection (Yielding a concentration of 0.5 mg/mL)... In small divided doses (0.1 - 0.2 ml) administer dose subcutaneously around the site... within 12 hours of extravasation.

canonical_statement: For infants, children, and adolescents, the policy limits phentolamine to 0.1-0.2 mg/kg or 5 mg total, dilutes 5 mg in 10 mL 0.9% sodium chloride to 0.5 mg/mL, clears the catheter with phentolamine before removal, and administers 0.2 mL subcutaneous divided doses around the site within 12 hours.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Dose should not exceed 0.1 to 0.2mg/kg or 5 mg total... Dilute 5 mg in 10 ml 0.9% Sodium Chloride... Inject phentolamine to clear the IV catheter, then remove the catheter... In small divided doses (0.2 ml) administer dose subcutaneously around the site... within 12 hours of extravasation.

canonical_statement: For adults, the policy dilutes phentolamine 5 mg in 10 mL 0.9% sodium chloride to 0.5 mg/mL, uses a small amount to clear the IV catheter before removal, and administers 0.2 mL subcutaneous divided doses around the site within 12 hours.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Adults... Dilute 5 mg in 10 ml 0.9% Sodium Chloride injection (Yielding a concentration of 0.5 mg/ml)... Inject a small amount of phentolamine to clear the IV catheter, then remove the catheter... In small divided doses (0.2 ml) administer dose subcutaneously around the site... within 12 hours of extravasation.

canonical_statement: For topical nitroglycerin treatment, the policy specifies nitroglycerin 2%, a 1-inch strip applied to the ischemic site, repeatable every 8 hours if necessary.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Topical Nitroglycerin 2%, 1-inch strip applied to the site of ischemia. Can repeat every 8 hours if necessary.

canonical_statement: The policy recommends local comfort measures according to the treatment table or patient preference when unspecified, including warm or cold compresses and limb elevation; ICN/SCN should not receive a compress.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Apply local comfort measures per table below or if not specified per patient preference (e.g., warm or cold compress, limb elevation)... ICN/SCN: Do not apply a compress

canonical_statement: For contrast-media extravasation, the policy directs clinicians to contact the provider and follow unit guidelines; if discovered after discharge from the area, the unit where the event occurred should be notified.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Contact provider and follow unit guidelines for care of contrast extravasation. Unit where extravasation occurred should be notified, if extravasation is found after discharge from that area.

canonical_statement: The policy calls for WOC consultation for every ICN/SCN extravasation, for pediatric nonblanchable erythema and edema after extravasation, and for adult wounds caused by extravasated medications that produce skin necrosis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: ICN/SCN: Consult the WOC Team for any extravasation occurrence... Peds: Consult the WOC Team for all non blanchable erythema and edema... Adult: Consult the WOC Nursing Team for wounds resulting from the extravasation of medications that cause skin necrosis.

canonical_statement: The policy lists as reportable conditions extravasation of a known vesicant or corrosive medication, increasing redness/induration/ulceration, increasing drainage from an ulcerated area, and temperature above 38.5°C orally in adults or above 37.1°C axillary in neonates and pediatrics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Reportable Conditions: Extravasation of known vesicants or corrosive medication... Increasing size of redness, induration or ulceration... Increasing amount of drainage... Temperature > 38.5 degrees C orally for adults and >37.1 degrees C axillary in neonates and pediatrics.

canonical_statement: For a warm dry compress, the policy specifies 15-20 minutes four times daily for the first 24-48 hours and states that warmth is intended to increase local blood flow and alter medication viscosity to enhance removal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Apply warm pack for 15 – 20 minutes four times per day for the first 24 – 48 hours... Warm compresses will encourage local blood flow and modify viscosity of the medication to enhance drug removal

canonical_statement: For a cold compress, the policy specifies at least 15-30 minutes four times daily for the first 48-72 hours and states that cooling is intended to reduce inflammation/pain and limit spread of the extravasated medication.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Apply cold compress for at least 15 – 30 minutes four times per day for the first 48 – 72 hours... Cold compresses are recommended to prevent further inflammation/pain and limit the spread of extravasated medication.

canonical_statement: For Acyclovir extravasation, the DUHS policy recommends a warm compress outside ICN/SCN, Hyaluronidase as the antidote/treatment, and no adjunctive or alternative treatment is listed.
